1.title: Formula Workshop
1.text: Welcome to Module 13, the formula workshop. Calculation questions are a minority of the exam, but they are quick points when the formulas are automatic. In Part 1, we work through the schedule, cost and risk formulas, using numbers from our microgrid. Part 2 covers people, value, contracts, quality and flow metrics.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where the numbers appear. The Process domain is forty-one percent of the exam, and this module touches four of its tasks. Task five, procurement, for contract and make-or-buy formulas. Task six, finance, for earned value, risk and value measures. Task eight, schedule, for estimating and the critical path. And task nine, status, for metrics. Most exam items are scenario judgment. The formulas are the quick points, so make them automatic.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Work schedule problems: estimates, probability and the critical path. Work cost problems: earned value, the estimate at completion and the to-complete index. Calculate expected monetary value and read a decision tree. Compare investments with net present value, internal rate of return and payback. Use the contract, statistics and agile formulas. And pick the right formula from the assumption words in the question.

1.title: How to Approach Any Calculation Question
1.text: Use the same six steps every time. One, find what is asked: a value, a decision or an interpretation. Two, list the data with units, and spot distractors, which are extra numbers. Three, find the assumption words in the stem. Four, write the formula, then compute, keeping fractions until the end. Five, sanity-check the direction, the sign and the convention. Six, choose the closest option, rounding once. If the numbers do not give a unique answer, follow the stated assumption.

1.title: Case Check-In: The Numbers
1.text: Here are the microgrid numbers we will use. The canopy construction package has a budget of four million dollars, and we will check its status. The commissioning sequence has five activities. The utility interconnection review has a three-point estimate in weeks. And there are a few risks and options. The numbers are for practice, and they sit inside the fourteen point two million dollar budget.

1.title: Estimating Duration
1.text: Three ways to estimate duration. Effort divided by people times availability: a hundred and twenty person-hours, with two people each seventy-five percent available, takes eighty elapsed hours. Parametric estimating multiplies quantity by hours per unit: forty drawings at twelve hours each is four hundred and eighty hours. Analogous estimating uses the actual of a similar earlier activity, adjusted for known differences. It is quick but less accurate. The effort formula is exam practice.

1.title: Three-Point Estimates
1.text: The interconnection review has an optimistic estimate of six weeks, a most likely of nine, and a pessimistic of eighteen. The triangular average, the one PMBOK 8 prints, adds the three and divides by three: eleven weeks. The PERT or beta estimate weights the most likely value by four and divides by six: ten weeks. That one is exam practice. The standard deviation is pessimistic minus optimistic, divided by six: two weeks, with a variance of four. For a path, add the expected durations, and take the square root of the summed variances.

1.title: Standard Deviation and Probability
1.text: Use the normal curve. About sixty-eight percent of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean: eight to twelve weeks here. About ninety-five percent fall within two: six to fourteen. And about ninety-nine point seven percent fall within three. For the chance of finishing by a date, compute z as the deadline minus the expected duration, divided by the standard deviation. A twelve-week deadline gives z of one, about eighty-four percent. A path with a lower mean but a larger spread can be riskier. The standard deviation bands and the z rule are exam practice.

1.title: Critical Path: The Day-1 Formulas
1.text: PMBOK 8 starts the project on day one. In the forward pass, early start is the latest early finish of the predecessors plus one, and early finish is early start plus duration minus one. In the backward pass, late finish is the earliest late start of the successors minus one, and late start is late finish minus duration plus one. Total float is late start minus early start, or late finish minus early finish. Free float is the successor's early start, minus this early finish, minus one. The critical path is the longest path, and it has zero total float.

1.title: Critical Path Worked Example
1.text: Here is the commissioning sequence. Foundations take four days and are followed by canopy steel, six days, and battery installation, eight days, in parallel. Both precede commissioning, three days, then the grid test, two days. In the forward pass, A runs days one to four, and C runs five to twelve. D runs thirteen to fifteen, and E runs sixteen to seventeen. The critical path is A, C, D, E: seventeen days. B finishes on day ten but has until day twelve, so it has two days of total float.

1.title: Total Float and Free Float
1.text: Total float is how long an activity can slip before the end date moves. It is late start minus early start, zero on the critical path, and negative when a constraint is violated. Free float is how long it can slip before the next activity moves: the successor's early start, minus this early finish, minus one. For canopy steel, thirteen minus ten minus one is two days. Free float is never more than total float. And remember, the critical path is the longest path, not the shortest. It can change after compression.

1.title: Compression: Crashing and Fast Tracking
1.text: Crashing adds resources to save time. The extra cost per day is crash cost minus normal cost, divided by the days saved. Crash only critical activities, cheapest per day first. Commissioning costs eighteen hundred a day, foundations twenty-four hundred, the grid test twenty-five hundred, and battery installation three thousand. Canopy steel has float, so do not crash it. Two days saved costs four thousand two hundred, and three days costs six thousand seven hundred. Fast tracking overlaps activities and adds risk. A lead lets a successor start earlier, a lag adds waiting time, and durations never include them. The crashing cost formula is exam practice.

1.title: Earned Value: The Measures
1.text: Earned value starts with four measures. Planned value is the authorized budget for the work scheduled to date: one point six million for the canopy package. Earned value is the budget authorized for the work actually performed: one point two million. Actual cost is what was incurred for that work: one point five million. And the budget at completion is the sum of all budgets, the cost baseline: four million. Earned value measures work in budget terms, not value to the customer.

1.title: Variances and Indices
1.text: Four formulas. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: minus three hundred thousand, so we are over budget. Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value: minus four hundred thousand, so we are behind. The cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost: zero point eight, or eighty cents of value per dollar spent. The schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value: zero point seven five. For both indices, above one is favorable.

1.title: Earned Value Curves
1.text: Picture the three curves at the data date. Planned value is highest, at one point six million. Actual cost is next, one point five. Earned value is lowest, one point two. Earned value below planned value means behind schedule. Earned value below actual cost means over budget. Here both indices are below one. Before reacting to a low schedule index, check the critical path, because slow non-critical work may not threaten the end date.

1.title: Choosing the EAC Formula
1.text: Choose the estimate at completion by the assumption. If current cost performance will continue, divide the budget by the cost index: four million over zero point eight is five million. If the variance was a one-off, add the remaining planned work to the actual cost: one point five plus two point eight is four point three million. If the original plan is no longer valid, add a bottom-up estimate to complete to the actual cost. And if cost and schedule both affect the rest, divide the remaining work by cost index times schedule index: six point one seven million.

1.title: ETC, VAC and TCPI
1.text: Now forecast the rest. Estimate to complete is the estimate at completion minus actual cost: five minus one point five is three point five million. Variance at completion is the budget minus the estimate at completion: minus one million. The to-complete index is remaining work over remaining funds. To meet the budget, two point eight over two point five is one point one two: twelve percent more efficient. To meet the estimate, two point eight over three point five is zero point eight. Above one is harder. Percent complete is thirty, spent thirty-seven and a half, planned forty.

1.title: Reserves and the Cost Baseline
1.text: Here is how the budget builds up. Work package estimates, plus a contingency reserve for known risks, make the cost baseline. Add a management reserve for unforeseen in-scope work, and you get the funding requirement. Contingency is inside the baseline. Management reserve is outside it. That is why a draw on contingency does not change the baseline, but a release of management reserve needs the approved process.

1.title: Expected Monetary Value
1.text: Now risk. A qualitative score is probability times impact. Expected monetary value is probability times the impact in money. Threats are negative and opportunities are positive. A late permit with thirty percent probability and a hundred thousand impact is minus thirty thousand. Battery rework, ten percent of two hundred thousand, is minus twenty thousand. A utility rebate, twenty percent of fifty thousand, is plus ten thousand. The net is minus forty thousand, and the threats alone are minus fifty thousand, so about fifty thousand of contingency covers the threats.

1.title: Decision Tree
1.text: A decision tree compares options. Option X, a larger battery reserve, costs four hundred thousand. It has a sixty percent chance of a million in avoided outage losses, and a forty percent chance of two hundred thousand. That is six hundred eighty thousand, less the cost: plus two hundred eighty thousand. Option Y, the standard reserve, costs two hundred thousand, with fifty percent of seven hundred thousand and fifty percent of a hundred thousand: plus two hundred thousand. Choose X, the higher expected value. PMBOK 8's own example picks a plant upgrade at forty-six million.

1.title: Is a Response Worth Buying?
1.text: Is a response worth buying? Suppose a threat has a twenty-five percent chance of an eighty thousand penalty: an exposure of twenty thousand. A response costing fifteen thousand cuts the probability to five percent, which leaves four thousand. The response removes sixteen thousand of exposure for fifteen thousand, so it is worth doing. Compare the cost with the reduction in exposure, not with the whole exposure. A contingency reserve can be a percentage, a fixed amount, or the result of a quantitative analysis.

1.title: Schedule, Cost and Risk Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for schedule, cost and risk. Read the assumption before choosing an estimate-at-completion formula. Mind the direction: above one is favorable, and negative variances are bad. The to-complete index is remaining work over remaining funds, so do not invert it. Under the day-one convention, early finish is early start plus duration minus one. The critical path is the longest path, and it can change after crashing. Expected monetary value signs: threats are negative, opportunities positive. And round at the end, without mixing percent and decimal forms.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. The method: find the ask, list the data, spot the assumption, write the formula, check, and choose. For schedule: the triangular and PERT averages, the day-one critical path, float, and crashing the cheapest critical activity first. For earned value: the variances, the indices, four estimate-at-completion formulas and the to-complete index. Contingency sits inside the baseline. For risk: expected monetary value, decision trees, and responses that are worth their cost. And the traps are direction, assumption and convention. In Part 2, we cover people, value, contracts, quality and flow metrics.

2.title: Communication Channels and Capacity
2.text: Part 2 starts with people. Communication channels equal n times n minus one, divided by two. Four people have six channels, six have fifteen, eight have twenty-eight, ten have forty-five, and twelve have sixty-six. Channels grow quadratically, not in step with the headcount. Capacity is people times available days times a focus factor: six people for ten days at zero point seven is forty-two person-days. Utilization is productive hours over available hours: thirty of forty is seventy-five percent. PMBOK 8 asks you only to consider the number of channels. The formula, capacity and utilization are exam practice.

2.title: Value Measures: Decision Rules
2.text: PMBOK 8 names these value measures but prints no formulas, so the formulas are exam practice. Net present value is the sum of discounted cash flows minus the investment. Accept if it is above zero, and choose the higher one among alternatives. Internal rate of return is the rate where the NPV is zero. Payback is investment over net annual inflow. It ignores the time value of money and later cash. Discounted payback is later than simple payback. Return on investment is net benefit over cost. And a benefit-cost ratio above one is acceptable.

2.title: NPV Worked Example
2.text: Two battery add-on options, at a ten percent required rate, in thousands. Option A invests a hundred and returns forty, fifty and sixty. The present values add to one hundred twenty-two point eight, so the NPV is plus twenty-two point eight. The IRR is about twenty-one point seven percent, and the payback is two point one seven years. Option B invests seventy and returns forty, forty and twenty: NPV plus fourteen point four, IRR twenty-two point seven percent, payback one point seven five years. Choose A. It adds the most value, even though B has the higher IRR and the shorter payback.

2.title: Costs That Matter and Costs That Do Not
2.text: Six related ideas. A sunk cost is already spent, so ignore it when deciding whether to continue. Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, and it belongs in the choice. Break-even is fixed cost divided by price minus variable cost. For lease or buy, set the two costs equal: sixty thousand plus two thousand a month equals five thousand a month, so twenty months. Straight-line depreciation is cost minus salvage value, over useful life. And present value is future value divided by one plus the rate, to the power of the years. These ideas are exam practice, not PMBOK 8 formulas.

2.title: Contract Formulas
2.text: Contract formulas. In a fixed-price contract, the price is fixed: the seller keeps savings and bears overruns. In a cost-reimbursable contract, the price is actual cost plus a fee, and the buyer carries the cost risk. Time and materials is hours times rate, plus materials. In a fixed price incentive fee contract, the seller's fee is the target fee plus the seller's share of the saving or overrun. The price is capped at the ceiling. The point of total assumption is the ceiling price minus the target price, divided by the buyer's share, plus the target cost. PMBOK 8 describes target-cost contracts that share savings and overruns, but these formulas are exam practice.

2.title: Target-Cost Worked Example
2.text: Take a commissioning support contract. Target cost is two hundred thousand, target fee twenty thousand, ceiling two hundred fifty thousand, shared eighty-twenty between buyer and seller. At an actual cost of two hundred thirty thousand, the seller's fee is twenty thousand minus twenty percent of the thirty thousand overrun: fourteen thousand. The buyer pays two hundred forty-four thousand. The point of total assumption is two hundred fifty minus two hundred twenty, over zero point eight, plus two hundred: two hundred thirty-seven thousand five hundred. Above it, the seller bears every extra dollar.

2.title: Quality Statistics
2.text: Quality statistics. About sixty-eight, ninety-five and ninety-nine point seven percent fall within one, two and three standard deviations. Control limits sit at the mean plus or minus three sigma: a mean of fifty and sigma of two give forty-four and fifty-six. The rule of seven says seven points on one side of the mean are a pattern to investigate. Cp is the specification range divided by six sigma: one point zero here. Cpk uses the nearer limit, so an off-center mean of fifty-two gives zero point six seven. Six Sigma means about three point four defects per million.

2.title: Agile Flow and Status Metrics
2.text: Agile and flow metrics. Forecast the finish by dividing remaining points by average velocity: a hundred and forty points at twenty a sprint is seven iterations, fourteen weeks. Little's law says cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput: fifteen items in progress and five done a week gives three weeks. Lead time runs from request to delivery, cycle time from start to done. WSJF divides cost of delay by job size. And the Net Promoter Score is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors: fifty minus thirty is twenty. PMBOK 8 names the Net Promoter Score. The velocity forecast, Little's law, weighted shortest job first and the NPS formula are exam practice.

2.title: Formulas by Approach
2.text: Formulas depend on the approach. Predictive work uses the critical path, float and PERT for schedule. It uses earned value for cost, expected monetary value and simulation for risk, and NPV at the gates. Agile work uses velocity forecasts and burnup for schedule, burn rate per iteration for cost, backlog items for risk, and value per iteration. Hybrid work uses milestone dates from the critical path, with iteration forecasts inside, and a mixed dashboard. A fixed-price government contract may mandate earned value, while a small agile team may need only velocity.

2.title: Which Formula? Cue Words
2.text: Look for cue words. Current performance will continue: budget over the cost index. The variance was a one-time event: actual cost plus the remaining budget. The original plan is no longer valid: actual cost plus a bottom-up estimate. Cost and schedule both affect the rest: divide by the product of both indices. A PERT or beta estimate: weight the most likely value by four and divide by six. And choose the better investment: the higher net present value, ignoring sunk cost.

2.title: Value, Contract and Flow Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for formulas. Control limits sit at the mean plus or minus three sigma, and Cpk uses the nearer limit. Contingency is inside the baseline, and management reserve is outside it. Channels grow quadratically. Net present value beats internal rate of return and payback when choosing, and sunk costs are ignored. Above the point of total assumption, the seller bears every extra dollar. And earned value is work done in budget terms, not value delivered. Round at the end, and pick the closest option.

2.title: Quick Reference: Schedule and Cost
2.text: Here is a quick reference for schedule and cost. Variances: CV is EV minus AC, SV is EV minus PV, and VAC is BAC minus EAC. Indices: CPI is EV over AC, SPI is EV over PV. Four EAC formulas. ETC is EAC minus AC, and TCPI has two forms. Critical path: early finish equals early start plus duration minus one, and late start equals late finish minus duration plus one. Three-point: triangular divides by three, PERT weights the most likely by four and divides by six. And crashing: crash cost minus normal cost, over days saved.

2.title: Quick Reference: Risk, Value, Contracts and Flow
2.text: Quick reference for the rest. Risk: EMV is probability times impact, a decision tree sums the branches less the cost, and respond only if the cost is below the reduction. People: channels are n times n minus one over two, and capacity is people times days times the focus factor. Value: NPV, IRR, payback, ROI and the benefit-cost ratio. Decisions: the higher NPV, ignoring sunk cost. Contracts: the fee formula and the point of total assumption. Statistics: the bands, the control limits and Cp. Agile: forecast iterations, Little's law and the Net Promoter Score.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap the module. The method: read the assumption first, then write the formula. Schedule and cost: the critical path, earned value, four estimate-at-completion formulas and the to-complete index. Risk: expected monetary value, decision trees, and responses that are worth their cost. Value: the higher net present value wins, and sunk costs are ignored. Contracts and flow: the point of total assumption, velocity forecasts and Little's law. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A package has a budget at completion of 600,000. At the status date, earned value is 240,000 and actual cost is 300,000. The overrun came from a one-time equipment failure, and the remaining work will go as planned. What is the estimate at completion? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The variance was a one-off, so future work goes at the planned rate. EAC equals AC plus BAC minus EV. That is 300,000 plus 360,000, or 660,000. Dividing by CPI assumes the overrun continues. 600,000 ignores the overrun. 360,000 is only the remaining work.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Task P takes 3 days and precedes Q, which takes 5 days, and R, which takes 2 days. Both Q and R precede S, which takes 4 days. Using the day-1 convention, what is the total float of R? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. R starts on day 4 at the earliest, and S starts on day 9. So R's late finish is day 8 and its late start is day 7. Seven minus four is three. R is not critical because Q is longer. 2 is its duration. 4 forgets the minus one in the day-1 convention.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Option 1 costs 20,000 and has a 50% chance of returning 60,000 and a 50% chance of returning 10,000. Option 2 costs 10,000 and has a 70% chance of returning 25,000 and a 30% chance of returning 5,000. Which is better by EMV? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Option 1 is 30,000 plus 5,000 minus 20,000, or +15,000. Option 2 is 17,500 plus 1,500 minus 10,000, or +9,000. The higher EMV wins. A smaller investment does not decide it. 35,000 ignores the cost. Positive EMVs are not equal.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A project invests 80,000 and returns 44,000 at the end of each of the next two years. The required rate is 10%. What is the NPV, and what should the team do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The present values are 40,000 and 36,364, a total of 76,364. That is below 80,000, so the NPV is minus 3,636, and the project should be rejected. 8,000 ignores discounting. Zero is wrong arithmetic. 76,364 is the present value, not the NPV.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A project has a budget at completion of 400,000, earned value of 100,000 and actual cost of 150,000. The team wants to finish within the original budget. What is the TCPI, and what does it mean? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. TCPI to meet the BAC is 300,000 divided by 250,000, or 1.20, so the remaining work must be done 20% more efficiently. 0.67 is the CPI. 0.83 inverts the ratio. 1.50 divides AC by EV, which is not the TCPI.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. A one-off variance means actual cost plus the remaining planned work. Question two: D. Total float is late start minus early start: seven minus four is three. Question three: A. Pick the higher expected monetary value, after deducting the cost. Question four: C. Discount the cash flows, then subtract the investment. Question five: B. The to-complete index is remaining work divided by remaining funds. That completes Module 13. Next, Module 14 covers the question types, the interactive formats, time management and the final steps of preparation. See you there.
